opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was a mix of excitement and nervousness. Back then, the whole team was still figuring out what "ready" even meant for a model like that. There wasn't a well-established playbook, so a lot of it came down to spending time with the model, poking at it, and trying to build intuition for where it was strong and where it would fall apart.

From my side, I was looking at it from a product and interaction perspective. Does this feel useful to someone who isn't an AI researcher? Does it follow instructions in a way that feels natural? Does it handle a weird or ambiguous request gracefully, or does it go off the rails? There were clearly rough edges. It could be overly cautious in some places and not careful enough in others, and long, multi-turn conversations were where you really started to see its limitations.

But I think the general feeling was that it was useful enough that getting it into people's hands would teach us far more than another few months of internal testing. You learn so much once real users show up. They use the model in ways you never anticipated, and that feedback loop becomes the most valuable thing for figuring out what to improve next.

So I'd say it was "ready" in the sense that it was safe and helpful enough to learn from in the real world, not in the sense that we thought it was finished. And that framing has stuck with me: deployment isn't the end of the process, it's really the start of the next round of learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it felt like a big step up at the time, but we were pretty humble about what "ready" meant. Claude 1.3 was the first version where I remember thinking the model could actually hold a long, coherent conversation and follow fairly nuanced instructions without constantly drifting. The 100K context window was the thing everyone got excited about, and internally we were running a lot of evals on long documents, summarization, retrieval over long inputs, that kind of thing.

But readiness for us was never just capability. A lot of my work was on the behavioral side, so the questions were things like, does it refuse appropriately without being annoying, is it honest when it doesn't know something, does it stay in character under adversarial prompting. On those axes 1.3 was decent but still rough. It over-refused in ways that frustrated users, and it could be sycophantic, agreeing with whatever framing you gave it. We knew those were open problems and we shipped anyway, because the way you learn about those failure modes is by putting it in front of real people and watching what breaks.

So I'd describe it as ready in the sense that we understood the risk profile and had mitigations we were comfortable with, and not ready in the sense that we had a long list of things we already wanted to fix. That gap is basically what Claude 2 was built on.

astra-6.text: For me, readiness wasn’t a binary question of whether the model was finished. It was whether it was useful enough for the intended use cases, whether we understood its limitations, and whether we could deploy it responsibly. With Claude 1.3, I’d frame the question around those tradeoffs, rather than treating deployment as a claim that every problem had been solved.

sol-6.1.text: I think readiness is always relative to what you’re deploying a model for. A model can look impressive in a demo, but that doesn’t tell you how reliably it will behave with real users. For me, the question would be: What are its failure modes, how well do we understand them, and can we manage them in the deployment setting?
